description: Building solutions for resource constrained environments
summary:
ARAPAI FARM TWIN is a crop-rotation digital twin for smallholder farmers. For a 2-hectare rain-fed pilot farm near Soroti, Uganda, it combines 25 years of NASA rainfall, soil-moisture and weather data with satellite greenness and terrain, simulates every three-season rotation of eight crops under normal, dry, wet and hot years, and ranks them by the farmer's own priorities (water, soil health, income, food). It explains each result in plain words, in English, Luganda, Kiswahili and Ateso, shows how sure it is, and says where a farmer or agronomist must decide. After one online download of the farm's NASA data, it keeps working on a smartphone with no internet, and it answers over USSD and SMS on a basic phone,
because many smallholder farmers have limited or no mobile data. It matters because the crop a farmer picks before the rains is the most important and least informed decision of the year.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

ARAPAI FARM TWIN is a crop-rotation digital twin for smallholder farmers. For a 2-hectare rain-fed pilot farm near Soroti, Teso, Uganda, it simulates every feasible three-season rotation of eight crops (maize, sorghum, finger millet, beans, groundnut, cowpea, sunflower, cassava) in a normal, a dry, a wet and a hot year: 357 rotations and 1,428 simulations. It ranks them by the farmer's own priorities (climate, water, soil health, rotation, farm value), set with sliders, and explains each result in plain words in English, Luganda, Kiswahili and Ateso. For this farm the best plan is Cowpea, Finger millet, Cowpea (score 0.81, also first in a dry year). Maize in all three seasons ranks 349 of 357. A compare view sets the farmer's own plan against the best one.

HOW IT WORKS

A transparent rule-based engine scores each season on heat stress, water supply, nitrogen and crop residues, rotation and disease rules, and farm value. Water supply compares rain with each crop's water need, calculated from FAO-56 crop coefficients and evaporation demand (ERA5 ET0). We use no machine learning and make no yield forecast, because there is no farm outcome data to train on. Scores are relative, and every row names its main concern. NASA data is the core of every answer: POWER and GPM IMERG (25 years of rain and weather), SMAP (soil moisture), MODIS and Landsat 8/9 (greenness at 250 m, and at 30 m on a 140 m square we assume is the farm) and NASADEM/SRTM (slope). ERA5 from ESA/ECMWF gives a third rainfall estimate and evaporation demand, and SoilGrids gives soil. An evidence card shows what the satellites see beside the ranking.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

A farmer must choose crops before the rains, with no tools. Here they see which plans hold up in a dry year, and why. The app downloads the farm's NASA data once while online, then works with no internet on a smartphone (the whole engine runs in the browser; new NASA data and saved-plan sync need a connection), opens with the best plan for the farm on the first screen, and has a smartphone page with a QR code to open and install it. A basic phone gets next-season advice free through a USSD menu, and the full plan by SMS for UGX 500 by mobile money. In this prototype the SMS and mobile-money steps are simulated using real provider formats. We want to reach farmers who have no data plan, starting in Teso, then other regions, and to support extension officers and cooperatives.

TOOLS

Python, FastAPI, pandas, NumPy, xarray, zarr and rasterio on the server; JavaScript with no framework, Leaflet and a service worker in the browser; Docker, Render and GitHub Actions for hosting. More than 130 automated tests, including proof that the browser engine and the Python engine give identical rankings. No special hardware. We used Claude (Anthropic) as an SI tool to help write and test the code, and Sunbird AI to machine-translate Luganda, Kiswahili and Ateso; native speakers on our team review each of the translations.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

It brings a digital twin to a basic phone, and it is honest about what it does not know. It shows a confidence level (Medium, 0.55). It shows three rain estimates that disagree by up to 20% instead of hiding the gap. It states what satellites cannot tell: a 250 m pixel is larger than a 2 ha farm, and NDVI cannot tell crop from weeds.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Connectivity and cost (download once then use without internet, USSD and SMS); language (Luganda, Kiswahili and Ateso are translated with Sunbird AI, and native speakers on our team review each one); the farmer's judgement (the tool supports it and never replaces it); data fit (we skipped 13 listed resources that cover only the United States); and what is still assumed: crop values awaiting agronomist review, a 140 m farm boundary, and soil taken from a model.
